\chapter{Noon and Midnight}
\label{ch:hi-noon-and-midnight}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say noon and midnight in Hindi and explain the old three-hour pahar hidden inside \hi{दोपहर}.}

Say \hi{दोपहर} as 'two pahars' and \hi{आधी} \hi{रात} as 'half night', contrasting one built on an old time-unit with one built plainly.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{दोपहर} \hi{आधी} \hi{रात}]{\hi{दोपहर}, \hi{आधी} \hi{रात} — noon by an old clock, midnight fully transparent}

\label{lesson:HI-C17-dopahar-aadhi-raat}



\begin{quote}
Hindi's word for noon hides a whole traditional timekeeping system inside it — one very different from hours and minutes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{दोपहर} — \textquotedblleft{}two pahars\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} (\emph{dopahar}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{noon, midday}\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two} (\emph{do}) + \textbf{pahar}.\textquotedblright{} A \textbf{\hi{पहर}} (\emph{pahar}, from Sanskrit \emph{prahara}) is a traditional Indian unit of time, roughly \textbf{three hours} long, with the day traditionally divided into eight \emph{pahars} (four for daytime, four for night), counted from sunrise. Noon falls right around the end of the \textbf{second} daytime \emph{pahar} after sunrise — so \emph{do-pahar}, \textquotedblleft{}two pahars {[}in{]},\textquotedblright{} became the everyday word for midday. (This traditional pahar-based account is the standard one, though — as with any folk-timekeeping etymology this old — treat the exact number of pahars as the general shape of the story rather than a precisely dated fact.)

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{आधी} \hi{रात} — fully transparent \textquotedblleft{}half night\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\hi{आधी} \hi{रात}} (\emph{ādhī rāt}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{midnight},\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{half night}\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\hi{आधी}} (\emph{ādhī}, the feminine form of \textbf{\hi{आधा}}, \emph{ādhā}, \textquotedblleft{}half\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\hi{रात}} (\emph{rāt}, \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}). No erosion, no double meaning — structurally identical to Latin's \emph{media nox} and Spanish's \emph{medianoche}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pahar\textquotedblright{} — a traditional \textasciitilde{}3-hour watch — then \textquotedblleft{}do-pahar,\textquotedblright{} two pahars, noon
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ādhī rāt\textquotedblright{} — half night, midnight
  \item the contrast — dopahar counts an old time-unit; ādhī rāt is plainly \textquotedblleft{}half\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} literally mean, and what's a \emph{pahar}? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Two pahars}\textquotedblright{} — a \emph{pahar} being a traditional \textasciitilde{}3-hour time-unit, with noon falling around the end of the second one after sunrise.) What does \textbf{\hi{आधी} \hi{रात}} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Half night}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ādhī} \textquotedblleft{}half\textquotedblright{} + \emph{rāt} \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} fully transparent, just like Latin's \emph{media nox}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la]{\hi{ल} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:HI-S121-letter-la}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \hi{◌ु} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ल}}
\textbf{\hi{ल}} — \emph{la}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{l}, it is \textbf{la}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a clockwise open left loop
  \item an up-right diagonal arm
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \hi{ल} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{अलविदा}} — goodbye (alvidā — a final farewell, Persian/Arabic-derived)
  \item \textbf{\hi{मिलेंगे}} \emph{milenge} — (we) will meet
  \item \textbf{\hi{फिर} \hi{मिलेंगे}} — we'll meet again (goodbye)
  \item \textbf{\hi{कल} \hi{मिलते} \hi{हैं}} — see you tomorrow (and the \hi{कल} puzzle)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ल}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the open lower-left tip, curve up and clockwise around the left loop, and finish at the inner junction
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at that junction and sweep the diagonal arm up-right to the right stem
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified four-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source writes the same parts in a stem-first order.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ल}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 11 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \hi{ल} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{अलविदा}  ·  \hi{मिलेंगे}  ·  \hi{नमस्ते}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ल} three times, saying \emph{la} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \hi{ल} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \hi{ल}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{la}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
